rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own split-plot field experiment (SDI vs DI, 3 N rates, 5 reps) at KARE 2013-2015 with harvest yield data. Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 3 - in 2013 prime and subprime fruit weights differed significantly between SDI and DI (SDI higher, letters a/b); in 2015 subprime yield differed between DI and SDI; total yield never significantly different.
rows.notes: Single site (Hanford sandy loam, one cultivar), single method (harvest yield) so no triangulation or representativeness. Q4 doubt: the study measures soil nitrate profiles (Fig. 7) and leaf N by irrigation type (Fig. 5) and suggests N placement near roots explains higher N productivity under SDI, but the pathway to the prime/subprime yield difference is asserted rather than measured, so answered no. Yield results carry only letter groupings at P=0.05 (no SD/CI reported for yields). Note the 2015 subprime difference favoured DI, not SDI.

rows.evidence: Q1: own field experiment (Sections 2-3). Q2: Section 3.7 and Table 8 - residual weed biomass sampled 28 Aug 2013 was 81 g/m2 under SDI vs 569 g/m2 under DI, significantly lower (P=0.0001); authors state SDI resulted in reduced weed pressure compared with DI. Q8: Section 3.7 - weed mass was not measured in other growing seasons, only observed; measurement was taken after herbicide burn-down.
rows.notes: Q3 doubt: infrared surface temperature was significantly higher under SDI and correlated with weed biomass (R=-0.636), plus photographic observation in 2012 (Fig. 8), but these are proxies/qualitative observations rather than an independent quantification of weed pressure, so answered no. Mechanism (dry soil surface under SDI) is not measured. Only means and P-values/letters, no dispersion.

rows.evidence: Q1: own field experiment with metered applied water and lysimeter ETc (Sections 2-3). Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 4 - water productivity for total yield was consistently higher in SDI (60.4, 61.0, 59.7 kg/ha/mm) than DI (51.5, 53.4, 55.8) in 2013-2015, explained by higher average SDI yields and lower applied water in SDI; Table 1 shows SDI received 584-843 mm vs DI 645-932 mm.
rows.notes: The lower water application to SDI was imposed by design (DI deliberately given ~10% more water to compensate for surface evaporation and weed water use), not a measured saving; soil evaporation under DI was not measured, so no intermediate variable (Q4 no). Authors say additional study is required to determine if further savings are possible, which is treated as a further-research statement rather than a stated limitation. WP compared statistically only across years; no dispersion reported for SDI vs DI WP.

rows.evidence: Q1: own field experiment (Sections 2-3). Q2: Section 3.4 and Tables 3-4 - average yield was consistently higher in SDI than DI in all three years (e.g. total 35,263 vs 33,210 kg/ha in 2013), though total yields were not statistically different; prime fruit yield significantly higher under SDI in 2013; Conclusions note a consistent non-statistical yield advantage of SDI.
rows.notes: Same profile as LIT_0113_08: single site and crop, one method, no dispersion for yields (letters only). The higher yield claimed in the passage is mostly a non-significant numerical difference, which the authors state. Q4 doubt as noted for the other yield row.

rows.evidence: Q1: own field experiment with metered irrigation (Sections 2-3). Q2: Section 3.4 and Table 4 - water productivity (yield per mm applied) was consistently higher under SDI than DI in 2013, 2014 and 2015 for total production, attributed to higher SDI yields and less applied water.
rows.notes: Water productivity, not a physiological WUE, is what the study reports. Applied-water difference between systems was set by design (DI given ~10% more). Single site, one method, no dispersion for the SDI vs DI WP comparison.

rows.evidence: Q1: own field experiment (Sections 2-3). Q2: Section 3.7 and Table 8 - weed biomass after herbicide burn-down was 81 g/m2 under SDI vs 569 g/m2 under surface drip, significantly lower (P=0.0001). Q8: Section 3.7 - authors state weed mass was measured only in 2013 and merely observed in other seasons.
rows.notes: Weed biomass quantified on one date in one season at one site; IR surface temperature correlation and 2012 photographs are supporting observations, not an independent quantification (Q3 no). No dispersion statistics reported.

rows.evidence: Q1: own field experiment (Sections 2-3). Q2: Section 3.4 and Tables 3, 4, 6 - average yields were consistently higher under SDI than DI in all three years (not statistically different for total yield; prime fruit significantly higher in 2013), and water productivity and N productivity (2013, 2014) were higher under SDI.
rows.notes: Single site, single crop and cultivar, one measurement method, plot scale. Yield differences between SDI and DI were mostly numerical, not significant, as the authors state. Only P=0.05 letter groupings reported for yields; no SD/CI. Q4 doubt: soil nitrate and leaf N measured but the pathway to yield is asserted.

notes: Full text appears complete. Single-site, three-year split-plot orchard experiment on Hanford sandy loam in California; lysimeter data (drainage, soil matric potential) were measured only under SDI. Figures 5 and 6 report standard errors for leaf and fruit N, but no dispersion is given for yield, water productivity or weed biomass results.
